1	# The library
2	
3	The library is `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`, without the compiler's own files there:
4	
5	- In `Library/`: the interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary.fss` and `.fsi`, and its other components. The compiler's `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerAlgebra` and `CompilerSystem` are not part of it. `FortressAst.fss` and `.fsi` are generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`: edit that file, never these two.
6	- In `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`: `FortressBuiltin`, `NativeArray` and the rest. The compiler's `CompilerBuiltin` is not part of it.
7	- `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType`, the top type, belongs to both libraries. After an edit to it, also take the compiled path's step (`build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library").
8	- `Library/incomplete/` is not on the source path (`default_repository/configuration`), so no program can import what it declares. Nothing that the suites or the model program run imports `Library/GeneratorLibrary.fss` either. Before you cite a declaration as the library's way, check that a running program can reach it.
9	
10	## How loops and reductions call the library
11	
12	The desugarer, which both paths share, turns these forms into calls of the library:
13	
14	- `for x <- g do b end` becomes `g.loop(fn x => b)`, a call of the generator's `loop` method. Each further generator nests one more `loop` call inside.
15	- `while x <- e do b end` becomes `while __whileCond(e, fn x => b) do end`. `if x <- e then ... end` becomes a call of `__cond`.
16	- A comprehension or a big operator, such as `SUM`, becomes a call of `__bigOperator`, whose argument calls `__generate` on each generator. So does a big operator inside another: no desugaring calls the library's `__bigOperator2`.
17	
18	These functions work on the library's generators and reductions: `trait Generator` and `trait Reduction` in `FortressLibrary.fsi`, and `RangeInternals.fss` for ranges. `FortressLibrary.fss` also defines `__loop`, but no desugaring calls it. So a failure inside a loop or a reduction is most often in the library's code, and its fix is a library edit.
19	
20	## The curator's decisions on the library
21	
22	- Scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` only. A range over another integer type is a static error, and walk stops when it builds one. Write a wider counter as a `ZZ32` loop that widens its index.
23	- `ZZ32` and numerals convert into `RR64` implicitly. `ZZ64` converts into `RR64` only explicitly, by `asFloat`.
24	- For arithmetic that wraps on overflow, use the wrapping operators ∔ `DOTPLUS`, ∸ `DOTMINUS` and ⨰ `DOTTIMES`. Parenthesise every such expression fully, because their precedence is stated only among themselves.
25	- `SUM` and `PROD` are generic over `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`. Write the element type wherever generators stand in brackets, also where the generators, the body or a declared type fix it: `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. The checker refuses a call without it (ledger row 731). Walk runs such a call at its value's declared type, or else at the join of its elements' run-time types. An empty `SUM` with no static argument written and no declared type gives the integer 0, and an empty `PROD` the integer 1, whatever the body's type (ledger row 716). With a static argument written that is not a number type, such as a user group, an empty or filtered `SUM` ends in `CastError` (ledger row 436).
26	- An indexed type's index parameter is bounded by `Index` (`revival-changes.md`, "Traits and objects"). `BoundedRange[\I\]` cannot take the bound, because the open range `(:)` stays a range over `Any` (P-56). So its `atMost(n: I): FullRange[\I\]` has the condition `where { I extends Index }`, which each call must meet (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi`). A type whose static parameter is a range's index type takes the bound too, as `UniformDistribution[\T extends Index\]` over a `FullRange[\T\]` (`Library/Random.fsi`).
27	- An array's `fill` takes a value, and its `tabulate` a function of the index: `array[\ZZ32\](4).fill(0)`, `array[\ZZ32\](4).tabulate(fn (i:ZZ32):ZZ32 => 10 i)`. The factories that take a function are `tabulatedArray1` to `tabulatedArray3` and `tabulatedVector`.
28	
29	## Designing a change
30	
31	- Put each extension into this library, outside the compiler's files. This includes an extension that only the model program needs.
32	- Fix a gap in the library, not by a workaround in the program that meets it. Take the design from the library's practice as well as from the specification's text. If the two disagree, do as `specification.md`, "When the text and an implementation disagree", says.
33	- If a rule of the language or the checker refuses the way that you want, find how the library writes that kind of thing. Do the same. The checker's refusals of this library reach you through your brief, or through a run of the count stage (`compiler.md`): `fortress typecheck` checks against the compiler's prelude.
34	- When you add a method, make it dotted or functional as its family in the library does. If the family shows no practice, follow the team's proposal, which no program can import (`Library/incomplete/Collection.fss`): an updater, a getter or a setter, indexing included, is dotted, and every other method is functional.
35	- A new functional method reserves its name in every program that imports the library. The phase that binds names then refuses each program that names a variable or a parameter after it: "Variable even is already declared."
36	- A `fail` without a static argument has the result type `Any`. Where it must have a type, write the static argument, as `strToInt` calls `fail[\ZZ32\]`.
37	- A dotted method shadows a top-level function of the same name (`overloading.tex`, "Principles of Overloading").
38	- In an api, declare each top-level function and each member of a trait or object at the header that the component gives it. A function's header is its name, its static parameters with their bounds, its modifiers, its `throws` clause, its parameters' modifiers and types, and its return type. A function's parameters' names and a `where` clause do not count, but each static parameter's name counts (ledger row 836). Give an object's value parameters the api's names, because they are its fields (`compiler.md`, "Traps of the compiled path"). In the cases below, change the component's header to the api's, not the api's to the component's. The examples are in `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi` and `Library/FortressLibrary.fss`.
39	  - The member's body already answers the api's type. `RR64`'s `opr |\self/|`, `opr |/self\|` and `truncate` answer `ZZ64`, because they call `Float`'s natives, which answer `ZZ64` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss:184-191`).
40	  - The api cannot name the component's type. `Array2`'s and `Array3`'s `bounds` and `zeroIndices` answered types of `RangeInternals`, which depends on this api. They now answer the api's `CompactFullRange` types, which those types extend.
41	  - The api's type is wider, and the overrides and bodies use only that type. `DelegatedIndexed`'s `generator` answers the api's `Generator[\E\]`, as `FlatString`'s override does.
42	
43	  In the api, write `abstract` on each member that the component leaves without a body.
44	- The compiled checker's export check matches each api member with a component member of the same name and header. It matches these members in these ways:
45	  - A field, as `x: ZZ32` in an api's trait: by a component field of its name, its type and its modifiers other than `var`. A component's getter does not match it, so declare a field in the component too (ledger row 842).
46	  - An object's value parameter: by its type and its modifiers other than `var`, but not by its name.
47	  - A getter written `abstract`, as `abstract getter one(): T`: by a component getter at its header, or by a component field of its name and type that is neither `hidden` nor `private`. A `hidden` field has no getter.
48	  - Another member written `abstract`: by a component member at the api's header, with a body or without one.

50	  Each entry of the check's error names a trait or object and only its first member that differs. After you fix that member, check again to see the next. These steps run the check:
51	  - For a component of a compiled program or test: `fortress compile`.
52	  - For the one library's `FortressLibrary` component: the count stage (`compiler.md`, "The checker's time").
53	  - For the other thirteen components that the gate's distance stage checks: that stage. When a rung needs it, the brief gives its command.
54	  - For another component of the one library: no step, until the switch-over.
55	- A new overload can make walk refuse every program at load. `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks", lists what walk refuses.
56	- Write a new native as a public static method of a class under `nativeHelpers/`, and bind it with `builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.Class.method")`. Both paths run it. Give it the Java types that carry the declared types (`interpreter.md`, "Natives"). Write a glue class under `interpreter/glue/prim/`, which only walk runs, only where no Java type carries a declared type, as for the bindings in `Library/Reflect.fss`. A native is an edit of Java: rebuild (`build-and-caches.md`, "Two layers of code"), and test it on both paths (`compiler.md`, "Natives").
57	- `interpreter.md`, "The model program", says how to check microGPT under walk.

59	## Editing
60	
61	A comment after a declaration that ends in an expression or a type becomes part of that declaration's source span. It also becomes part of the unambiguous name made from the span. So a comment-only edit changes the syntax tree. Before you compare parse trees or diagnostics across such an edit, map their positions back to the lines before the edit. Three removed scripts did this: `parse-compare.sh`, `ast-compare.py` and `remap-lines.py`. Print one with `git show ab067d9b6^:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/<name>`.

1	# The compiled checker, the code generator and the runtime
2	
3	**count stage**
4	: Script that runs the compiled checker over the interpreter's library, on the `FortressLibrary` component and the apis that it imports, and prints the errors in a table: `explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh`. Its total is the checker count.
5	
6	**distance stage**
7	: Stage of the gate that runs the compiled checker over fourteen components of the interpreter's library, `FortressLibrary` among them, runs each of the checker's steps on each component whatever the earlier steps report, and prints the errors in a table. Your brief gives its command when you need it.
8	
9	The code of this area is in these directories:
10	
11	- `scala_src/typechecker/`: the type checker, in Scala.
12	- `compiler/`: the disambiguator, the desugarers, overloading, `codegen/`, `NamingCzar` and `OverloadSet`.
13	- `runtimeSystem/`: `InstantiatingClassloader`, tasks and transactions.
14	
15	The phases' names in the code are parse, PREDISAMBIGUATEDESUGAR, DISAMBIGUATE, GRAMMAR, PRETYPECHECKDESUGAR, INTEGERLITERALFOLDING, TYPECHECK, DESUGAR, OVERLOADREWRITE and CODEGEN.

17	## What the two paths share
18	
19	After the phases, each path has its own code for these:
20	
21	- Values: walk's `interpreter/evaluator/values/` (`FInt`, `FFloat`), and the compiled `compiler/runtimeValues/` (`FZZ32`, `FRR64`).
22	- Number natives: walk's glue classes, in `interpreter/glue/prim/` (`Int.java`, `Long.java`).
23	- Dispatch: walk searches at run time, in `OverloadedFunction`. The compiled path calls a dispatch method that `OverloadSet` generates.
24	- The run: `fortress run` starts a second JVM (`bin/run`), which never enters `Shell.java`.
25	
26	Both paths run the helpers, the public static methods of classes under `nativeHelpers/`.
27	
28	The phases differ too: walk turns off some desugarings that the compiled path runs (`interpreter.md`, "Where a fix of walk belongs"). A fix of one of those desugarers changes only the compiled path.
29	
30	## The compiler's prelude, until the switch-over
31	
32	The compiled path uses the compiler's own prelude: `LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss`, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss` and `Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss`. `Library/CompilerSystem.fss` is the compiled path's `System`.
33	
34	Do not add a declaration to the three prelude files: they are deleted at the switch-over, and their tests stay. The one exception is the numerals: until then, the prelude's numeral types and its coercions from them follow `revival-changes.md`, "Numbers" (P-37). If a helper of `nativeHelpers/` that the one library binds is wrong, fix the helper's Java, even where the prelude binds it too. Do not edit the prelude's text: its binding then gives the fixed result. If a compiled test pinned the old result, change the test with the helper, as for any fixed defect.
35	
36	## What the compiled path cannot compile yet
37	
38	For a construct that it cannot compile yet, the code generator calls `sayWhat` or throws another `CompilerError`. Such a call or throw is a code-generator wall. The code generator has no case for these constructs:
39	
40	- `label` and `exit`, `spawn`, and `atomic` used as an expression;
41	- an object expression;
42	- an array literal, such as `[1 2 3]`.
43	
44	It compiles a local function as a closure, also one that calls itself or another local function of its block. It refuses these forms (ledger row 304):
45	
46	- a local function with static parameters of its own: 'Can't compile a local function with static parameters of its own yet';
47	- two local functions of one name in a block: 'Can't compile overloaded local functions yet';
48	- a local function with the `atomic` modifier: 'Can't compile a local function with this modifier yet'.
49	
50	A type assumption `e asif T` has the value of `e`, but the call around it chooses its declaration as if `e` were a `T`, a supertype of `e`'s type (`Specification/basic/expressions/type-annotation.tex`). The code generator compiles one at a dotted call's receiver, at a call of a functional method or an overloaded function whose every argument is an assumption, and elsewhere as the value of `e`. It refuses these forms (ledger row 818):
51	
52	- a call of a functional method or an overloaded function with an assumption at some of its arguments but not all: 'Can't compile a dispatched call whose arguments are not all type assumptions';
53	- a generic method on an assumed receiver: 'Can't compile a type assumption at the receiver of a generic method yet';
54	- a call of an overloaded generic function with an assumption at an argument: 'Can't compile a type assumption at a call of an overloaded generic function yet'.
55	
56	It also refuses a function or method with a contract (`requires`, `ensures`, `invariant`). It compiles a declaration whose own header or `extends` entry has a `where` clause, and emits nothing for the clause. A call of a function or method whose own clause introduces a `where`-clause variable, as `where [\nat n\]` does, links, but dies at run time with `NoClassDefFoundError` (ledger row 867). `compiler_tests/XXXWhereVariableCallCompiled.test` records it: copy its form for such a call. The disambiguator, which both paths run, drops a trait's or object's contract, so the code generator never sees one, and walk does not check one either (ledger row 781). It refuses a function or method with a modifier other than `getter`, `setter`, `io`, `private`, `abstract` and `test`, such as `override` (ledger row 650). A trait or object that extends a generic trait compiles with `Any` as the static argument. With `Bottom`, `Self` or an abbreviated type there, the code generator refuses the declaration. An abbreviated type is a short form, such as `RR64[3]` for an array type. With a tuple that holds `Any` there, the code generator crashes (ledger row 889).
57	
58	The compiler's prelude has no array types, only `ZZ32Vector` and `StringVector`. Its `for` loops, comprehensions and reductions work over `ZZ32` ranges only. Its reductions give a `ZZ32` or a `String`.
59	
60	Until the switch-over, a compiled test uses none of these. If a test needs one, write it as an `XXX` test that names the wall (`tests-writing.md`).
61	
62	## What the code generator does
63	
64	- It emits no primitive `double` arithmetic.
65	- It runs a program's own `coerce` from a numeral once for each place where the numeral is written, in the component class's static initializer, except where the place's type names a type parameter (below). So a coercion that raises stops the program before `run()`. A test of it sets `run_exits_nonzero=true` (`tests-writing.md`).
66	- The class loader rewrites a template's bytes with ASM. The emitted classfiles stay at version 1.6, because this rewriting keeps no stack-map frames. Do not raise the version.
67	- The `value` modifier adds the mark interface `ValueObjectMark` to the object's class. The compiled `SEQV` (`nativeHelpers/equality.java`) reads the mark. The modifier does not inline or unbox the fields.
68	- An array of `RR64` values is to be stored as an unboxed `double[]`. The code generator does not build it yet. If your task touches how arrays are stored, print the two POSITIONS entries on arrays first (about 2 KB):
69	
70	      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'positions:array is stored as' 'positions:array design'
71	
72	## The runtime
73	
74	- The class loader is `runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java`. The revival has changed it for sizes and for the lock on a class's first load (ledger row 417). Before you investigate a failure while a class loads, read ledger rows 408 and 559, which name it (`records.md`, "Reading the record").
75	- The compiled code keeps each mutable variable in a cell (`compiler/runtimeValues/MutableFValue.java`). Before each read and write of the cell, the generated code asks `BaseTask.inATransaction()` (`runtimeSystem/`). Inside an `atomic` block, the access goes through the transaction. So the transaction tracks the variables that the block touches. From the switch-over, it also tracks each element of the one library's arrays, by array and index: `compiler/runtimeValues/FortressArrayStore.java` calls the transaction's methods `TXReadSlot` and `TXWriteSlot`. Walk does not run this class, so test an edit of it with `ArrayStoreJUTest`, beside it.
76	
77	## Natives
78	
79	`import java com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.{...}` in a `.fss` file binds static Java methods over plain Java values.
80	
81	A body `builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.Class.method")` binds one such method, a helper, too. In a compile, at the parse, the compiled path, and not walk, rewrites the body as a call of the method through a generated `import java`, with `self` first in a trait or object (`compiler/BuiltinPrimitiveRewriter.java`). The checker then checks the declaration against the method's Java signature. In a compile, it reads `int` as `ZZ32`, `long` as `ZZ64`, `float` as `RR32`, `double` as `RR64`, `boolean` as `Boolean`, `String` as `JavaString`, `BigInteger` as `ZZ` and `Object` as `Any` (`NamingCzar.fortressTypeForForeignJavaType`). The compile stops in these cases:
82	
83	- If the string is in that package but names no public static method: 'builtinPrimitive names no static helper: …'.
84	- If the string names a glue class or anything else outside that package: 'Variable builtinPrimitive is not defined.'
85	- If the declaration has a varargs parameter: the same message (ledger row 849).
86	- If the declaration is a local function or a method of an object expression: the same message. The rewrite reaches only a component's declarations and the members of its traits and objects (ledger row 865).
87	
88	The rewrite runs only in a JVM that has made a Fortress repository of the compiled path, the compiler's store of components, not this git repository. Walk's repository switches it off again. `fortress compile` makes one, and so do `disambiguate`, `grammar`, `desugar` and `typecheck` (`Shell.compilerPhases`). `fortress parse` and `fortress api` make none, so they rewrite a body only after a compile in the same JVM (ledger row 882). Alone, they pass a misspelt helper. Test a binding with `compile`. In a suite, the result of `parse` or `api` depends on whether a compile ran earlier in the same JVM.
89	
90	To test a helper on the compiled path, write a compiled test whose own declarations bind it, as `compiler_tests/NativeHelperBindingCompiled.fss` does. Until the switch-over, a compiled test cannot reach the interpreter's library's bindings.
91	
92	The count stage and the distance stage check the interpreter's library with the same rewrite. There, the checker differs from a compile in these ways:
93	
94	- A string that names a glue class, or a declaration with a varargs parameter, does not stop the check. The body stays a call of `builtinPrimitive`, typed at the declared result type, and no Java signature checks it (ledger row 849).
95	- The checker reads a helper's Java types as the interpreter's library's types: `String` as `String`, not `JavaString`, and the rest as in a compile.
96	- A component that imports a DSL grammar is parsed by other code (`GraphRepository.syntaxExpand`), which does not rewrite its bindings. So, as for a glue class, no Java signature checks them.
97	- The count stage checks only the `FortressLibrary` component's bindings. A binding of another component, as `FortressBuiltin`'s, only the distance stage checks.
98	
99	The checker, in a compile and in both stages, reads `int` as `NN32` or `Char`, and `long` as `NN64`, only for six transfer helpers with fixed names (`NamingCzar.java:373-384`, `:494-503`). Where a binding gives a parameter, `self` or the result the type `NN32`, `NN64` or `Char`, or a parameter or `self` the type `UnsignedLong` (the one library's object that extends `NN64`), and the helper has `int` or `long` there, the rewrite passes that value through the matching transfer helper. A result declared `UnsignedLong` gets none. `self` gets a transfer helper only in a method of one of these four types itself. The transfer helpers return their argument unchanged. So the checker accepts such a binding whatever helper it names, a signed one included, as `simpleIntArith.intLT` for `NN32`'s `<`. If you move a binding over these types onto a helper, test it on both paths at values where a signed and an unsigned reading differ (2^31 and above for `NN32`, 2^63 and above for `NN64`), as `compiler_tests/NativeHelperFamilyNN32Compiled.fss` and `tests/NativeHelperFamilyNN32Walk.fss` do. If the class has more than one method of the helper's name and number of parameters, the rewrite adds no transfer helper. The checker then reports 'Could not check call to function builtinPrimitive_<Class>_<method>', followed by '… is not applicable to an argument of type …'.
100	
101	The wrapper generator wraps every method of a class that it is given, the private methods too. If a type has no Fortress counterpart, it fails the whole import. So give every method of a helper class a signature that maps to Fortress, also a private method. In the count stage and the distance stage, a type maps only if the interpreter's library declares it. So there, a binding stops its component if any method of its helper's class has a type that only the compiler's prelude declares. The distance stage then counts the component as a stopped target. `nativeHelpers/systemOps` is such a class: its `getArgs` answers `StringVector`, so the message is 'FortressBuiltin.StringVector is undefined.' (F-321). Bind a helper of another class.
102	
103	## Traps of the compiled path
104	
105	- The compiler's prelude declares `print`, `println` and `String`'s `||` at `Object`, not `Any` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:37`, `:55`, `:61`). So until the switch-over, the checker refuses a generic that prints a value of a type parameter written without a bound, or concatenates it onto a `String`. The message names `Object`, as 'Object->() is not applicable to an argument of type T.' does for `println`. In such a generic of a compiled program or test, write `T extends Object`. The generic then takes no tuple, function or `()`. The one library declares these operations at `Any` or `String`, so do not change its text for this limit. The prelude's `||` takes the string first only, so `c || s` for a `Character` value `c` is refused (ledger row 965). Put a string first, as `("" || c) || s`.
106	- A `try`'s `forbid` clause lists exception types: an exception of a listed type that no `catch` clause took is wrapped in a `ForbiddenException`, which the `try` throws. A `try`'s `finally` clause does not run when an exception leaves the `try` block: one that no `catch` clause takes, or that `ForbiddenException` (ledger row 890). So write no compiled program that relies on `finally` after an exception leaves the `try`. A test that needs it is an `XXX` test (`tests-writing.md`). In a `try` nested in another `try` of one body, the outer `try`'s `catch` clause is matched first (ledger row 888). A `try` whose block can throw, with a `finally` clause and no `catch` or `forbid` clause, fails with a `VerifyError` at class load (ledger row 891).
107	- Numerals and sizes depart from `revival-changes.md`, "Numbers", in these ways:
108	  - At a place whose type names a type parameter of its generic declaration, a numeral's coercion runs at each evaluation (ledger row 957). If the body needs the value at one instance only, bind it once, at a top-level variable whose type names no type parameter.
109	  - A numeral coercion whose body spawns a task fails the component class's load: 'Thread cannot be cast to FortressTaskRunner' (ledger row 971). An operator or an argument list over two calls of the program's own functions spawns, as `small(n) - small(m)` does. Bind each call in a statement of its own, as `a = small(n)`, then `b = small(m)`, then write `a - b`.
110	  - Until the switch-over, `RR64` converts only an `RR32` and a numeral with a radix point, and `RR32` only such a numeral. So `r: RR64 = 3` is refused, and so is a `ZZ32` value where an `RR64` is expected (ledger row 442). Write `3.0`, and `i.asRR64` for a `ZZ32` value `i`.
111	  - A `nat` or `int` parameter of 2^31 or more, used as a value, raises a `java.lang.Error` that no `catch` sees (ledger row 962). Assert no value for it in a test.
112	  - As a `typecase`'s selector, a numeral keeps its own type, as `NaturalNumeral[\1,10,7\]`, so `typecase 7 of ZZ32 => ...` is refused as unreachable (ledger row 963). Bind the selector to a variable first, as `x = 7`, then write `typecase x of ...`.
113	- A `typecase` tuple pattern with an untyped binder, as `(x, y: ZZ32)`, stops the code generator: 'typcase match failure!' (ledger row 964). Give each binder a type.
114	- An api and the component that implements it must have the same name. If there is none, the link fails ("Could not find an implementation for API"), and the run dies with `NoClassDefFoundError`.
115	- The compiled dispatch ignores the contravariance of a parameter of arrow type. The property `fortress.disable.contravariance` is true by default, so `OverloadSet` passes no variance. If a compiled call with function arguments picks another declaration than walk does, look here first.
116	- A clean link does not prove that every call has its method. Two calls die at run time with `NoSuchMethodError`:
117	  - a call of a functional method of an object that a trait's `comprises` clause lists, on a value whose static type is the object. An example is `num(R)`, where `trait Q comprises { R }` declares `abstract num(self): ZZ32` and `object R extends Q` gives its body. Call it through a value typed as the trait, as `q: Q = R` and then `num(q)` (ledger row 815);
118	  - a read of an exported object's value parameter, from a component that imports the api, where the exporting component names the parameter otherwise than the api. A value parameter is a parameter of the object's constructor, and also a field. An example is `Np(3).a`, where the api declares `object Np(a: ZZ32)` and the component `object Np(z: ZZ32)`. The export check compares no value parameter's name. Give each value parameter the api's name (ledger row 839).
119	
120	## The checker's gaps
121	
122	- Overloads: in its test of whether two domains exclude each other, the checker puts the meet of a static parameter's declared bounds in the parameter's place where the parameter is a whole parameter type, an element of a tuple or a member of an intersection or union (P-157). Inside a static argument, as `T` in `Box[\T\]`, the parameter stays. The paths differ on `tint[\T extends Red\](x: Box[\T\])` beside `tint[\T extends Blue\](x: Box[\T\])`, where `Red`, `Blue` and `Box` are objects. The checker refuses it, because `Box[\Bottom\]` lies in both domains, and walk loads it. No decision says which is right. Assert neither path's answer in a test (ledger row 786).
123	- A `where` clause's constraint: the checker checks a function's or functional method's constraint on its own static parameters at the call. At a dotted call, a candidate is not applicable where the receiver's static argument breaks the method's constraint. A trait's or object's own constraint is checked where its type is used, also at a constructor call; only the checker reads it, and the compiled code does not check it. A `where`-clause variable is a static parameter of the function's arrow type, inferred at the call. The checker does not yet check these, and no ledger row holds the first two:
124	  - at a dotted call, a constraint whose bound names the method's own static parameters or a `where`-clause variable;
125	  - at a type's use, a constraint whose bound names a `where`-clause variable;
126	  - a static argument written at a top-level call, against its parameter's bound (ledger row 470).
127	- Imports: `import A.{...}`, with the three dots written, imports every name of `A`. The overloading check also reads `A`'s declarations of a name that the component imports by name from another api. So `import A.{...}` beside `import B.{ pick }`, where both apis declare `pick(x: P)`, is refused: 'There are multiple declarations of pick' (ledger row 813). Leave the name out of the whole import, as `import A.{...} except { pick }`.
128	- An `except` clause leaves out each identifier that it lists, on both paths. Neither path leaves out an infix operator that it lists. So where a component lists `-` in `except` and declares its own `-` at the api's parameter types, the code generator stops. Walk runs the component's own `-` (ledger row 814).
129	- Conditional extension: the condition holds while the checker checks the `extends` entry itself, an object's value parameters and every member. It does not hold for the other `extends` entries, the static parameters, the declaration's own `where` clause, and the `excludes` and `comprises` clauses. The checker lets a member that it checked under the condition be called where the condition fails (ledger row 773).
130	- A `comprises` clause that lists a type at a `where`-clause variable, as `NatParam comprises { N[\n\] } where [\ nat n \]` or `AnyList comprises List[\E\] where [\E\]`: at a call, the checker gives the variable a fresh size or type, equal only to itself. Two values passed in one call get two. A fresh type is bounded by the binding and by the clause's constraints. The variable is in scope in the trait, except in its `extends` and `excludes` clauses. The checker gives no fresh type where it meets the trait as a supertype of another type. Where a generic type that the clause lists, as `List[\E\]`, gives the body of a member of the trait, the code generator crashes: 'E is not in the kind env' (ledger row 812). Where the variable is a size, a compiled call that passes a value of such a trait where a listed type is expected fails the JVM's verification (ledger row 307). Departures: a fresh type also under a function type's result (ledger row 751), none for an extender that the clause does not list (ledger row 752), and a crash at a call, from outside the trait, of a member whose type names the variable (ledger row 756).

132	## The `fortress` commands
133	
134	`Shell.java` dispatches `bin/fortress <command>`.
135	
136	- To see what an early phase makes of a program, stop after that phase: `parse` (a syntax check), `disambiguate`, `grammar`, `desugar` or `typecheck`.
137	- `unparse` prints the syntax tree back as Fortress source. Use it to see what a desugaring made.
138	- `link` links a compiled component (the `link` step of a compiled `.test` file). `api` writes a component's api. `test` runs a program's `test` declarations under walk.
139	- The command chooses the library. Walk and `test` call `Shell.useInterpreterLibraries()`. Every other command calls `useCompilerLibraries()`. Each call points `WellKnownNames` and `Types` to its prelude, and sets the desugaring switches.

143	    cd ProjectFortress
144	    # after an ant compileAll that started the caches again: the library order (build-and-caches.md)
145	    ../bin/fortress compile <path>/P.fss

184	The count stage takes `<out-file> <scratch>` and about 80 to 180 seconds, more under load. It can run past the Bash tool's 120-second limit, so run it in the background (`session.md`). 186	The checker checks every api first, and the component only if no api has an error. In each api or component, it stops at the first of its stages that finds errors. The stages run in this order (`compiler/StaticChecker.java`, `checkCompilationUnit`):

195

197	- `#stopped`, in place of `#total` and `#locations`: the errors came from a phase before the checker, such as the parse. The checker reported none and did not reach the component. The script exits 1, and the gate reads the table as red.

The coercion's body calls the type's constructor on values computed from the four numbers, as in `coerce[\nat n, nat m, nat r, nat v\](x: RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]) = Interval(roundDown(v, r, m), roundUp(v, r, m))`, and the compiler instantiates it for the numeral and folds it (P-176). No numeral value exists when a program runs: a numeral type has no getters, no `asFloat`, no `asString` and no `=` with a number type, and is written only as a coercion's or an operator's parameter type. A numeral has no sign: at a program's type `-3` is the type's own prefix `-` applied to the coercion's result for `3`, and a type without `-` refuses it; any other expression of numerals alone folds first (P-173) and reaches such a type only through its coercion from the folded value's type, such as `QQ` for `1/2`, since coercions do not chain. The design leaves out the binary chapter's numeral coercion and `opr ||` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/advanced-lib/binary.tex:1620-1662`). - P-37 **One library, the interpreter's, is the library that the compiler checks.** The interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`, becomes the compiled path's prelude in place of the compiler's own, and the compiled path reads the interpreter's library with it. Why: the switch-over spares porting the interpreter's library into the compiler's; the revival develops the checker until it accepts that fuller library. The curator sees the compiler's prelude, its own library files `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin` and `CompilerAlgebra`, as a bootstrap to remove. So no declaration is added to the compiler's prelude, and at the switch-over its three files are deleted and their tests kept (P-38 says which tests are respelled; F-293 holds the compiler's fourth file, `CompilerSystem`). The one exception is the numerals: until the switch-over the prelude carries the design of P-174 and P-176, so that both paths treat a numeral alike before it, and that copy goes with the prelude. The decision settles which files survive, not the designs inside them: the one library takes a design of the prelude's where it is the team's later decision, as it took the prelude's flat shape of the number types. This decision does not stop work on the code generator, which is compiler work under either library.

1	# The interpreter (walk)
2	
3	Walk's code is in `interpreter/`:
4	
5	- `evaluator/`: the tree walker.
6	- `env/`: the environments, which map names to values, and the wrappers that load components and apis.
7	- `rewrite/`: walk's own rewrite of the tree.
8	- `glue/`: the natives.
9	
10	## How walk evaluates a program
11	
12	After the phases (`SKILL.md`, "The phases"), walk rewrites each component in `interpreter/rewrite/`: it gives each reference to a name the lexical depth of its declaration. The evaluator looks up the name by that depth. The compiled path has no such rewrite.
13	
14	At a call of a generic function, walk infers the static arguments from the run-time types of the arguments (`interpreter/evaluator/EvaluatorBase.java`, `inferAndInstantiateGenericFunction`). Each static parameter gets an interval, from a lower to an upper bound, in a `LatticeIntervalMap` (`useful/`). A type in the domain of an arrow type, such as `T` in `T -> ZZ32`, is contravariant. So its bounds go into the dual map, `LatticeIntervalMapDual`: the same table, with the order reversed. `MakeInferenceSpecific` then makes the inferences more specific, in practice only in the dual map.
15	
16	Walk chooses a coercion by the value at run time. The specification and the compiled path choose it statically. Walk has no static types, so it cannot choose statically. The expected-failure tests `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXCoercionStaticRungC.fss` and `XXXCoercionStaticNarrowRungC.fss` record the difference.
17	
18	Walk departs from the rules of `revival-changes.md`, "Numbers", in these ways, until each fix lands. A test of one of these cases asserts the rules' answer, as an `XXX` test (`tests-writing.md`), unless the case says otherwise.
19	
20	- A float numeral to the left of an `RR32` operand runs `RR64`'s operator: for `a: RR32`, `2.5 + a` is an `RR64`, and `a + 2.5` an `RR32` (ledger row 958). Bind the numeral at `RR32` first, as `c: RR32 = 2.5`, then write `c + a`.
21	- A numeral with a radix point keeps only one of its leading zeros, so a coercion over `RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]` gets `n` = 2 for `00.5`, not 3 (ledger row 960).
22	- A `nat` or `int` parameter of 2^31 or more, used as a value, is a `ZZ64` (ledger row 962). Assert no value for it in a test.
23	- A numeral at `=` takes its default. So `u = 0` is `false` for a zero `u` of `NN32`, `NN64` or `RR32`, and so is `q = 0.5` for `q: QQ = 1/2` (ledger row 973). `u =/= 0` and `q =/= 0.5` are then `true` (ledger row 966). Bind the numeral at the type first, as `z: NN32 = 0`, then write `u = z` or `u =/= z`.
24	- A numeral that rounds to an infinity at `RR32` or `RR64` gives `Infinity`, with no error (ledger row 967).
25	- A numeral type written as a static argument, or as a type that an object or a trait extends, loads and runs, as `Wrap[\NaturalNumeral[\1, 10, 3\]\](3)` does (ledger row 974). The rules refuse both forms, as the compiled checker does: 'NaturalNumeral cannot be written in a program except as a parameter's type.'
26	- A body with a declared return type is not converted by coercion, except a numeral: `r(): Wide = NarrowOf(3)` returns the `NarrowOf` (ledger row 387). Write the value at the declared type.
27	
28	## Where a fix of walk belongs
29	
30	Both paths run the same desugaring phases. Inside them, switches in `Shell.java` decide which desugarings run. Walk turns off these desugarings, which the compiled path runs:
31	
32	- coercion;
33	- chained comparisons;
34	- compound and tuple assignment, and subscripts;
35	- case expressions, typecase and type ascription;
36	- the marking of a bodiless declaration as abstract.
37	
38	Walk evaluates those nodes itself, in `interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java` (`forChainExpr`, `forAssignment`, `forCaseExpr`, `forTypecase`, `forAsExpr`). It converts by coercion at dispatch, in `OverloadedFunction.bestMatchWithCoercion`. So if walk is wrong on one of these nodes, fix the evaluator, not the desugarer.
39	
40	An edit of a phase that both paths run, or of the desugaring switches, can change both paths. An edit under `interpreter/` changes walk only.
41	
42	## What walk checks
43	
44	Walk does not check static types (`SKILL.md`, "The phases"). The commands that stop after a phase, and `unparse`, use the compiler's prelude and the compiled path's desugaring switches (`compiler.md`, "The `fortress` commands"). So `fortress typecheck` does not check a walk program, and `desugar` or `unparse` does not print the tree that walk runs. That tree is the component's entry in `interpreter_cache/` (`SKILL.md`, "The caches").
45	
46	Under walk, the disambiguator, the phase that binds names, refuses a program's own top-level type that has the name of a type of `FortressLibrary`, such as `Index` or `Indexed`: "Type name may refer to: Index, FortressLibrary.Index". Give such a type another name.
47	
48	At load, walk checks the overload sets, some `comprises` clauses, inherited abstract methods and `override` declarations. It lifts each object expression to the top level as an object, which takes the static parameters of an enclosing generic function, and checks it as an object. It checks a trait or object with static parameters once, through a stand-in: one type for all its instances, with a symbolic type for each static parameter (`symbolicInstance` in `interpreter/evaluator/BuildEnvironments.java`). Through the stand-in, it does not check two functional methods whose parameter types mention a symbolic type. It makes no stand-in, and so checks nothing through one, for a declaration with an `opr` static parameter, or where its static parameters, `where` clause or `extends` clause raise an error at the symbolic types. It refuses:
49	
50	- two declarations of one name that its parameter-by-parameter check cannot order. It accepts them if `comprises` clauses cover the overlap. For every pair of functions of which at least one is generic, it checks the overloading rules of `SKILL.md`, "Fortress as a language", on their declared domains (`revival-changes.md`, "Dispatch and overloading"): the No Duplicates Rule, the Meet Rule and the Return Type Rule. So it refuses two whose declared domains are equal. The message names the rule: "fails because their parameter lists have the same types", "fails the Return Type Rule" or "fails the Meet Rule". Walk keeps the team's check and messages for the pairs below. The team's check looks for a position where the two parameter types neither nest nor exclude. If a parameter type there mentions a static parameter, the message is "at least one pair of parameters must have excluding types". If neither does, it is "are unrelated (neither subtype, excludes, nor equal) and no excluding pair is present". The pairs:
51	  - a pair with a varargs parameter;
52	  - a pair whose parameter lists differ in length, only where one of them has a varargs parameter. Walk checks no other pair of lists of different lengths;
53	  - a pair that is neither two generic declarations, nor a generic one beside a plain one, nor a generic function beside a generic trait's or object's functional method that has no static parameters of its own;
54	  - the instances of an explicit instantiation.
55	
56	  Where it reads exclusion over the whole tuple of parameter types, at the instance that the equalities force, it reads two parameter types that still mention a static parameter as excluding only where no instances of the two can meet. Walk departs from the rules in these cases:
57	  - At load, it does not check two functional methods of a generic trait or object on their declared domains. It compares them at each call, on the instance that the call makes. So such a pair that breaks the rules loads, and a call can fail with "Cannot find definition for method" (ledger row 780).
58	  - It refuses two generic functional methods whose declared domains lie one inside the other, in a type without static parameters (ledger row 779).
59	  - It refuses a pair whose overlap it finds only through an instance of a supertype, also where a third declaration covers the overlap (ledger row 539).
60	  - It refuses overloads on two instantiations of one generic type, as `g(b: Tg[\3\])` beside `g(b: Tg[\4\])` (ledger row 416).
61	  - Its parameter-by-parameter check reads an object type over a static parameter as excluding a type that one of its instances is or extends. So it loads `g[\T\](x: Box[\T\], y: ZZ32)` beside `g(x: Box[\ZZ32\], y: Any)`, which the Meet Rule refuses (ledger row 788).
62	  - It reads no `where` clause when it reads exclusion over the whole tuple. So it refuses such a pair where one declaration has a `where` clause of its own (ledger row 787).
63	  - It does not refuse a type that extends a self-typed trait `T[\A\]` and is not an `A` (`revival-changes.md`, "Traits and objects"). 64	  - It loads a generic top-level function whose declared domain lies inside that of a self-typed trait's functional method of the same name, where the Return Type Rule holds. 65	  - It loads a function over `Index` beside one over a pair whose element types neither lie below `Index` nor exclude it, which the Meet Rule refuses (ledger row 806).
66	  - It loads a type that provides two functional symbolic operators, such as two `||`, that break the Meet Rule for Functional Methods (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex`). The checker refuses the pair (ledger row 611).
67	
68	  The paths differ on `f[\T extends { K, R[\T\] }\](x: T)` beside `f(x: Z)`, where `K comprises { A, B, C }`, `Z excludes { A, B }`, and `C` is an object that extends `Z` but not `R`. Walk refuses the pair: "fails the Meet Rule". The checker reads the bounds, finds that no value lies in both domains, and accepts it. No decision says which is right. Assert neither path's answer in a test (ledger row 713).

70	- an overloaded function with one parameter of type `T`, where `T extends Any` is written: `f[\T extends Any\](x: T)`.
71	- an extender that a `comprises` clause of the program's main component does not allow. Walk does not yet check the library's clauses, another component's clauses or an object expression's clauses. Where a listed type names a bounded type `where`-clause variable, as `NBox[\E\]` in `comprises { NBox[\E\] } where [\E extends Number\]`, walk ignores the variable's bound, and runs `NBox[\String\]` (ledger row 754). 76	  - a generic trait or object that extends a type under a `where` clause.

## 11. Consequences talked through on 2026-11-09, 15:xx to 16:3x UTC

He confirmed each as a consequence of the design, not a choice ("There is no alternative here").

- The library's own number types take numerals by the same generic coercion as a program's type (the Draft: "Libraries define coercions from numerals to integers ... and rational numbers"). The compiler's folding for a built-in type is the folding of a constructor call whose result is a JVM `int`, `long` or `double`. A separate way in the compiler for the shipped numerics is a hole in the design.
- `-3` at a program's own type: the coercion receives the written numeral `3`; the type's own `opr -(self)` (the additive group's operation, `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:267-271`) applies to the result; both run once, when the class loads, so the whole `-3` at that place is one constant. A type without `-` refuses `-3`. Batch 29's fold, which hands the coercion a signed value (rows 961, 968, queue item 448), is wrong; the revised specification's sentence (`Specification/basic/expressions/literals.tex:215-218`) is right.
- `-2147483648` at `ZZ32`: the static expression folds exactly first, then converts (his 23:10 to 23:23 on 11-08, repair 3).
- `2 + 3` or `1/2` at a program's own type: by repair 3's "a written numeral only", only a written numeral goes through the numeral coercion; `2 + 3` is two `ZZ32` defaults added, `1/2` a `QQ`; the type takes them only through a coercion from `ZZ32` or `QQ`, and refuses them otherwise, since coercions do not chain.
- The `=` pairs between a numeral type and a number type, eleven each way as built: deleted with the run-time numeral objects. "It was a wrong choice and it gets deleted." The probe tests `u = 0` for `u: NN32`, the one use the prototype saw: the checker fixes `0` at `NN32` from the other operand and folds it.
- Walk: no checker, so it meets the numeral at run time. At a fixed type it converts from the four numbers once, at the first evaluation of the place; at no type, the default; at a program's own type it instantiates the generic coercion with the numeral's four numbers as the static arguments, as walk fixes static parameters from run-time arguments (the preamble's own words, `Specification/fortress/preamble.tex:134-136`), runs the constructor call once for the place and keeps the result. Row 486 (walk refuses a `nat` static parameter used as a value) stands in the way. A refusal at a type with no coercion from the numeral type comes at run time under walk until walk runs the checker (P-12).
- A bare numeral with no type defaults, so the team's `NumberPrintTest:16` (a 32-digit numeral printed as written) prints 16 digits: his bend of 22:40, recorded. microGPT's untyped hyperparameters read as `RR64` the same way.
- "Static constraints" (the preamble, `:35-37`): the specification's "It is a static error" rules, checked before a program runs by the team's checkers beside the type checker (`compiler/StaticChecker.java`). His compile-time range check on a numeral coercion is one such constraint; under walk none exists until P-12.
- P-37, which lets nothing be added to the compiler's prelude, gets an exception for the numerals, so that both paths do the same thing before the switch-over; the prelude's copy of the static numerals goes with the prelude at the switch-over (his word at 17:1x UTC on 11-09: "Of course, I'm making exception for the P37.").
- A static expression at a program's own type: repair 3's mix stands as the probe's default, the sign through the type's own `-`, every other static expression through a coercion from `QQ` or `ZZ`; explained to him at 17:0x; confirmed at 17:2x UTC on 11-09: "I don't want anything change. I want that behavior with sign and what we [took as] repair three from last night." The complex test's notation is `3 + 4 i`, `i` a constant of the type, juxtaposition as multiplication (20:11, 20:13 on 11-08); batch 29's `imaginary` is not it.
======
### The point for him in the morning

**Question 1 of the probe: `u = 0` for a zero `u: NN32`, and its kin (`w = 0` for an `NN64`, `0 = u`).** With the `=` pairs between the numeral types and the number types deleted ("It was a wrong choice and it gets deleted", SNAP `11. Consequences`), `u = 0` meets two declarations: the library's `=` over `Any`, which the numeral fits at its default `ZZ32` (P-173: at `Any` a numeral takes its default), answering `u SEQV 0`, `false`; and `NN32`'s own `=`, which the numeral reaches only by its conversion. The snapshot's section 11 gives `true`, "the checker fixes `0` at `NN32` from the other operand and folds it". The tree's rule that a declaration applicable without a coercion runs before one that needs it gives `false` (P-173's `gg(5, w)` by P-49; walk's `OverloadedFunction.bestMatchForNumeralsInternal`, PROBE `13. Questions`). The ways (PROBE `13. Questions`, question 1): (a) a numeral reaches a declaration by its conversion before one it fits only at its default, where that declaration is more specific, which changes the tree's rule and walk's dispatch; (b) `false`, strict equivalence of an `NN32` and a `ZZ32`; (c) the pairs kept, against his word. **Landed, not built further:** the probe's state. Under walk `u = 0` is `false`: the eight assertions of it and its kin move into `tests/XXXNumeralEqualsNumberWalk.fss`, which asserts the snapshot's `true` and expects its failure (PROBE `7. Step 6`), with a new ledger row; on the compiled path it is `true`, since the prelude declares no `=` over `Any` (PROBE `10. What was not built`). **Consequential:** each way reads P-173 or the snapshot anew.

Beside it, for the record and not for a decision: P-173 still says that a place fixes a type when its declared type "is a numeral type", which P-174 rules out, since a numeral type is written only as a parameter type; the patch refuses a binding at a numeral type on both paths (PROBE `1. Where the snapshot`). The record-landing workflow brings P-173 in line (section 6).

=====

## 10. What was not built

- A coercion declared in another component than the numeral's site, on the compiled path: the code generator inlines only a coercion it finds in the component it compiles (`numeralCoercionDecl`). Elsewhere the call stays at its site and the class loader instantiates the generic coercion, one class per numeral, with `v` among the stamped sizes, which `RTTIsize.of` holds as an `int`. Neither the one-method form nor a wider `RTTIsize` was built; no test reaches it.
- A site whose type names a type variable, as `m(): Gen[\T\] = 3` in `object Box[\T\]` (row 957's second case): not hoisted, as before.
- The type's `-` on a negative constant at a program's type runs at each evaluation on the compiled path; only the coercion is hoisted, where P-176 has the `-` run in the `static final` too. Under walk the whole constant is made once for the place.
- Under walk, `u = 0` for `u: NN32` and its kin give `false` (section 13, question 1). The compiled path gives `true` only because the prelude declares no `=` over `Any`.
- Under walk, a `where` clause refuses only when the place runs (P-176 until P-12), and a numeral type written as a variable's type is refused only when its binding runs.
- A numeral in a `case` expression's winning clause, an `if` without `else` or a `try` with a `finally` clause is converted by the old path, not in place; no test reached it.
- Only `where` comparisons of sizes are read; `where { v < 256 }`-style arithmetic is read with `+`, `-`, `^` and multiplication only.
- The specification is not revised: `Specification/basic/expressions/literals.tex` still states the field numerals (F-345), and Appendix I has no entry for the static numerals.
- Rows the prototype repairs but cannot close, since it lands nothing: 318, 362, 957 (first case), 961, 968, 969, 970, and row 513 for a numeral coercion.

## 11. Findings the record does not hold

2. The four numbers read as values inside a numeral coercion are `ZZ`; elsewhere a `nat` stays a `ZZ32` (P-173). The brief's "exact integers"; the alternative, every `nat` value a `ZZ`, changes P-173 and its tests.
3. At a built-in target the compiled fold is batch 29's, recognised by the target type; the checker reaches it through the library's generic coercion. 4. On the compiled path the coercion is inlined at its site, not compiled as one method that takes the four numbers as values (section 5 gives why).

## 4. Step 3: the checker

What was built:

- A numeral's type carries its four numbers as static arguments, `v` at any size: `3.125` is `RadixPointNumeral[\4,3,10,3125\]`, `3000000000` is `NaturalNumeral[\10,10,3000000000\]` (`impls/Misc.scala`, the literal cases; `compiler/Types.java`, `numeralType`). The four numbers come from one new helper that both paths and the code generator use, `nodes_util/NumeralNumbers.java`, a port of batch 29's reading in `Numerals.java`. The analyzer compares sizes by their `BigInteger` values already (`scala_src/typechecker/Formula.scala:120-131`), so `v` beyond 32 bits needed no change there. The kind check refused it: "Ill-formed static argument: 9223372036854775807", eight errors in five places; a numeral type's arguments and a numeral coercion's static arguments are now exempt (`TypeWellFormedChecker.scala`).
- Inference of a generic coercion's static arguments from the numeral's type is the checker's own static-argument inference (`CoercionOracle.checkCoercionTrait`, `inferStaticParams`); it worked unchanged. `getCoercionTargetsFrom`, which skipped every generic coercion, now admits one generic over a numeral's four numbers (`CoercionOracle.scala`), so a numeral still promotes a generic call (P-74).
- The range refusal as a static error: a coercion's `where` clause of size comparisons, as `where { v < 256 }`, is computed exactly at the inferred four numbers; a coercion whose clause fails is not a candidate, and the refusal reads "The numeral 300 does not meet the where clause of the coercion to Byte." (`CoercionOracle.whereHolds`, `numeralRefusal`). Only comparisons of sizes are read; any other constraint is left to the checks that read it. At the eight library types the range refusal is batch 29's, by the value (`NumeralConversion.outOfRange`), not by a `where` clause (section 12, decision 6).
- Inside a coercion over a numeral type, the four numbers read as values are `ZZ`, exact integers; elsewhere a `nat` read as a value stays a `ZZ32` (P-173): `KindEnv.getType` and `markExact`, set from the declaration's parameter type in `impls/Decls.scala`.
- A numeral has no sign. The fold (`compiler/desugarer/IntegerLiteralFoldingVisitor.java`) now marks its results by their text: prefix minus on a numeral as written keeps the written text after `-`, any other folded constant is written in parentheses, `(5)`. A radix-point numeral under a minus is folded the same way, its node holding the magnitude so that `-0.0` keeps its sign where it converts. At a library type the signed value converts directly, as before, so `-2147483648` at `ZZ32` folds exactly first. At a program's own type a negative constant is the type's own prefix minus on the coercion of the numeral as written: the checker checks that minus on a stand-in of the type and puts the coercion in its place (`STypeChecker.scala`, `coercions.negator`), with the component's own disambiguated prefix minus, which the fold now records per component (`prefixMinusOf`). A type without a prefix minus refuses it: "The numeral -3 at Plain needs a prefix minus on Plain, which it does not declare." Any other folded constant reaches a program's type only through its default's type (`CoercionOracle.buildCoercion`; `defaultFits` does the rest).
- P-173's default where nothing fixes a type is kept as it is. Two places changed because two numerals now have two types: an `if`, `case`, `try` or block whose results are numerals, alone or beside values that already fit, converts each numeral branch at the expected type in place (`numeralJoinInto`, `joinInto`, the `if`'s winning-clause path in `impls/Misc.scala`), and a tuple of numerals converts element by element in place (`buildCoercion`). Before, the checker coerced such a join or tuple as a whole, which ran a numeral's coercion at run time on an `IntLiteral` value; the static numerals have no value to run it on.
- Lines: `scala_src` and `compiler/Types.java`, "8 files changed, 316 insertions(+), 32 deletions(-)"; the fold and `NumeralNumbers.java`, "2 files changed, 161 insertions(+), 6 deletions(-)".

Measured (count and distance stages over the one library, timed by `references/compiler.md`): the first run after the change, "#total 9 / #locations 5" (1m10.783s), the eight kind errors and one tuple join; then "#total 0 / #locations 0 / #crash none", "real 1m43.093s". The final runs are in section 8.

    opr >=(self, other:T): Boolean = (self = other OR: self > other)
